name: Maya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a company that builds timber buildings off-site, so half my week's in the factory putting together wall panels and floor sections, and half's on site fitting them together on apartment blocks. In the factory there's already a big machine that cuts the timber from the drawings and a nailing bridge that fires the nails in rows. My job's the bit in between: checking, fixing the odd cut, fitting windows into panels, then on site guiding them off the crane and fixing them. I love site days when a whole floor goes up before lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology come into your day already?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere, really. I use an AI app every day to check drawings against what's on the bench and to make cut lists, and it translates for Bogdan and Ana, who are still learning English. I'm usually the one who gets asked when the machine software does something odd. I rent a flat with my friend Tash and cycle to the factory, and I've got about two and a half months' rent and bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd post something like, so much for the robot future, back to the nail gun. At work I'd still be showing people shortcuts on the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays pretty much as it is, which is fine. I like it. I'd just keep looking for small ways the tools could make things less boring, like cutting out the paperwork on deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep using the AI app for drawings and translating. I'd maybe go for the factory's supervisor role when it comes up next spring, since I already sort out half the software problems. And I'd keep saving a bit each month, maybe a hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bit flat. Like a film that everyone hyped and it was just all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be happiest at work if nothing much changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Ken, our oldest site carpenter, who still calls the crane radio the walkie-talkie. He'd be thrilled. Honestly I'd be glad for him, he's not got many years left and he'd rather not learn anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And you say you'd be disappointed. Is there a part of you that's relieved too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. There's always a fear that the thing you're excited about ends up eating your job. If it's just a nice tool, nobody I care about gets hurt.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed and post something like, so much for the robot future, back to the nail gun. At work I'd keep showing people shortcuts on the app.
S0.think: My job stays as it is, and that's fine because I like it. I'd keep looking for small ways tools could cut the boring parts, like delivery paperwork.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI for drawings and translation. Applies for the factory supervisor role next spring and saves about a hundred a month.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a hyped film that was only all right.
S0.quote: I'd post something like, so much for the robot future, back to the nail gun.
S0.fieldNote: Maya is the rare worker who'd be mildly let down if AI fizzled. She admits relief too, because no one she cares about would be hurt. She's already the informal tech helper in her factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if we share it. Faster building means more homes, and that's what this country needs. But I'd say the workers need a say in how the machines come in, not just the bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well out of it. I'm already the person who gets the machine back up and running. The ones I'd worry about are the lads who only do the nailing and lifting, because that's the first thing a robot arm takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss to send me on the course for the panel line robots, the one the machine supplier runs. I'd suggest we use a robot for the window fitting on the line, because it's the job that wrecks everyone's back. And I'd keep using AI for everything I can, maybe learn to set up the cut files myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Excited, with a little worry for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd suggest bringing in a robot yourself. How would that go down with the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well at first, I know. Ken would call me a traitor as a joke and maybe not as a joke. But I'd rather we choose where it goes and keep the people, than have head office pick for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in return for being the one who pushes the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pay bump for whoever learns to run it, and a promise nobody's let go because of it, just moved. I'd go to the union with that before I go to the boss. I'm not going to make myself the reason someone loses their job.

S1.say: I'd say this is good if it's shared, because faster building means more homes. But workers need a say in how machines come in, not just bosses.
S1.think: I'd do well, since I'm already the one who gets the machines running. I'd worry about colleagues who only do nailing and lifting, which a robot arm takes first.
S1.do: Asks to go on the machine supplier's robot course and suggests a robot for window fitting on the panel line. Learns to set up the cut files herself and takes a no-layoff deal to the union before the boss.
S1.feel: Excited, with a little worry for other people.
S1.quote: Ken would call me a traitor as a joke and maybe not as a joke.
S1.fieldNote: She'd bring automation in herself, but on terms she'd want agreed through the union first. Her progressive views show in her concern for colleagues who only do the heavy, repetitive work. She expects friction and isn't hiding from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and someone needs to slow it down until there's a safety net. I'd post about it, and I'd be at the union meeting. I'd probably say we need a basic income now, not after people lose their homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm better placed than most, but it'd still hit me. If AI can do any work, it can also fix the machine software, so my little advantage only lasts a year or two. With two and a half months saved, I wouldn't last long without a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd go all-in on whatever the factory needs to keep a human for, probably supervising and fixing the robots. I'd push my savings up, skip the cycling trip to the mountains Tash and I planned, and put that money away. I'd also go to the union and push for a deal that everyone on the line gets retrained, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd still feel like I had moves to make. I think I'd be busy rather than frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your advantage only lasts a year or two. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe I end up as a sort of babysitter for robots, the person who signs to say the building's safe. Or maybe there's no job and it's all about whether the government steps in. I hate not having an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Bogdan and Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd help them get on any course going, and translate for them if they need it. They came here for this work, and they've got less to fall back on than me. I'd feel responsible.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and needs slowing until there's a safety net. I'd post, go to the union meeting and call for a basic income now.
S2.think: I'm better placed than most, but if AI can fix machine software too, my edge only lasts a year or two. Two and a half months saved wouldn't last long.
S2.do: Goes all-in on supervising and repairing the factory robots, and drops a planned cycling trip to save the money. Pushes the union for a deal to retrain everyone on the line.
S2.feel: Anxious but busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: Maybe I end up as a sort of babysitter for robots, the person who signs to say the building's safe.
S2.fieldNote: Even this early adopter sees her edge running out fast in the two-year version. She keeps acting and keeps thinking of colleagues with less cushion. She openly doesn't know what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, so let's do it properly. I'd be pushing for the factories to share the gains, like shorter weeks for the same pay. I'd be quite loud about that online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me. I'd learn the robot side properly, maybe do a part-time engineering course, and be one of the people who sets them up and keeps them safe. What worries me is that the people who need the time most won't be given it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start a part-time course in construction engineering, two evenings a week. I'd volunteer for every pilot the factory runs. I'd go looking at other firms that are further ahead and see if I should move there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy underneath. Like being on a crane lift, you trust the gear but you watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving firms. Would you leave the people you've been defending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the contradiction, isn't it. I'd want to stay and help, but if a firm down the road is three years ahead, that's where I learn the most. Maybe I'd go and come back with what I learned, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a shorter week mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More time on the bike and probably a second skill. I've always wanted to learn furniture making properly, the slow kind. If robots build the flats, I'd still like to make a chair by hand.

S3.say: I'd say we have time to do this properly, so let's. I'd push for factories to share the gains, like shorter weeks for the same pay.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to learn the robot side properly. What worries me is that the people who need the time most won't be given it.
S3.do: Starts a part-time construction engineering course two evenings a week and volunteers for every factory pilot. Looks at firms further ahead and considers moving to one.
S3.feel: Mostly fine with a little unease underneath, like trusting the gear on a crane lift but watching it.
S3.quote: If robots build the flats, I'd still like to make a chair by hand.
S3.fieldNote: She notices the tension herself between defending her workmates and moving to a firm further ahead. Five years turns her plan from scrambling into a proper course. She keeps coming back to a wish to keep hand skills for their own sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make it good for everyone, if we're not lazy about it. I'd want apprenticeships for robot technicians and a law about sharing the gains. That's what I'd be posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I feel pretty good about it. I'd have time to become an engineer and still be in my thirties. I'd probably end up running a line of robots, and I quite like that idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start the engineering course and work out the cheapest way to do it, probably the one the company part-funds. I'd keep using every AI tool I can get, because that's how you learn what it's good at. I'd go to union meetings about apprenticeships for robot work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like the start of something, not the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people relax because it's ten years and then it sneaks up. Ken's retired by then, fine, but the lads in their forties won't be. If they don't start until year eight, it's the two-year version for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your job title to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something boring like line engineer. I'd want to still go on site sometimes, to see the floors go up. I don't think I'd ever get tired of that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to make this good for everyone if we're not lazy. I'd post about apprenticeships for robot technicians and a law on sharing the gains.
S4.think: I feel good about it, because I'd have time to become an engineer and still be in my thirties. I'd probably end up running a line of robots, and I like that idea.
S4.do: Starts the engineering course, ideally one the company part-funds, and keeps using every AI tool she can. Goes to union meetings about apprenticeships for robot work.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the start of something rather than the end.
S4.quote: If they don't start until year eight, it's the two-year version for them.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline suits her completely, and she's mostly looking forward. Her one fear is that others will put off acting until it's too late. She still wants to see the floors go up on site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even I couldn't keep up, and the people around me would have no chance. What would help is money while people retrain and a say for workers in where the robots go. Shorter weeks for the same pay would be the dream.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether people actually want to do the hard bits. I don't miss carrying window frames, and I don't think anyone would. The fear isn't losing the heavy lifting, it's losing the wage.

headlineQuote: The fear isn't losing the heavy lifting, it's losing the wage.
portrait: Maya Novak is a 27-year-old carpenter who splits her week between a timber-panel factory and apartment sites, and who already uses AI every day for drawings and translating for colleagues. She rents with a friend, cycles to work and has about two and a half months saved. She's calm when AI stays small or changes things steadily, and would even push for robots on the line if the union got a no-layoff deal. AGI in two years makes her anxious because even her edge runs out fast, but with five or ten years she plans an engineering course and feels hopeful. Her worry is mostly for colleagues with less to fall back on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even she couldn't keep up and the people around her would have no chance.
whatWouldHelp: Money while people retrain, a say for workers in where robots go, and ideally shorter weeks for the same pay.
